title: SYSK Selects: What was the most peaceful time in history?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun (originally March 2000) in which Josh and Chuck ask what the most peaceful time in history was. They open with the Vision of Humanity Global Peace Index (top and bottom countries, indicators, yearly rank changes), then weigh candidates: the Pax Romana (Gibbon's dating, Janus gates, Ara Pacis, rebellions and exceptions, Commodus ending it) and Genghis Khan's Mongol Empire (Nishapur massacre, postal system, legal protections, the gold-sack legend), rejecting both. They then turn to Steven Pinker's argument that violence has declined since hunter-gatherer times (Hobbes, state monopoly on violence, technology and connection, Peter Singer's expanding circle, medicine's effect on violence, the UN and common currency, in-group/out-group language). The episode ends with a listener mail from Aaron about public behavior and condoms in New York City, followed by sign-off.

entities.name: The Angels of Our Better Nature

segments.title: Selects intro and banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode, originally from March 2000, and recommends a related Pinker article. Hosts open with banter.

segments.title: Global Peace Index rankings
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Vision of Humanity Global Peace Index: the most peaceful countries (Iceland at number one, Western European countries in the top ten), the least peaceful (Somalia, Afghanistan, Sudan, Iraq, Congo, Russia, North Korea, Central African Republic, Israel, Pakistan), how civil wars shift rankings, the UK and US positions, and the indicators used.

segments.title: Pax Romana
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Pax Romana, dated by Edward Gibbon from roughly 27 BC under Augustus, the Gates of Janus and Ara Pacis as symbols, and popular rebellions and violence within the period. They conclude it was peaceful for the empire as a whole but violent for some, and consider it but are not persuaded it was the most peaceful time.

segments.title: Roman entertainment and the vomitorium
segments.summary: A digression on the vomitorium, which was an entrance and exit rather than a place for purging, and on excess among followers of Bacchus, plus brief talk of Caligula.

segments.title: Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire
segments.summary: The hosts consider Genghis Khan's Mongol Empire as a candidate. They recall the Nishapur massacre, then his later legal protections, freedom of religion, a postal system with relay stations, and the legend of a woman walking with gold. They reject it as most peaceful because of the killing needed to build the empire.

segments.title: Pinker on the decline of violence
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh present Steven Pinker's argument that violence has declined since hunter-gatherer times and the 20th century's wars. Factors discussed: media coverage, Hobbes and the state monopoly on violence, technology and connection, understanding of others, Peter Singer's expanding circle, medicine's effect on the value of life, and the UN, the EU, and common currency. They also discuss in-group and out-group language.
topics: The Better Angels of Our Nature

segments.title: Listener mail: condoms and public behavior in New York
segments.summary: A listener named Aaron offers a theory that New Yorkers engage in private behavior in public because of limited privacy, which relates to the earlier condom discussion.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank Aaron, invite listener contact through Twitter, Facebook, and email, and point listeners to the website.
